title: A New Radio to Overcome Critical Link Budgets

predicted_errors.error_location: Section V-1 (description of Fig. 2) vs. Section IV-A-2
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Section V-1 states: "The four possible symbol transitions for the leftmost subcarrier are shown in Fig. 2 ... The phase is changed by temporarily lowering the frequency." This contradicts the design rule established in Section IV-A-2, which states that for the rightmost subcarrier the frequency should be lowered and "For the leftmost subcarrier, this consideration holds vice versa" (i.e. the frequency must be *raised*, phase-shift set {+3π/2, +π, +π/2, 0}). It also contradicts the Fig. 1 description that "Changes are predominantly directed towards the center of the frequency band" (upward for the leftmost carrier).

The text says "during the sinusoidal phase, i.e. L_s ≤ s < SN − L_e", whereas Eq. (7) defines the sinusoidal interval as L_s ≤ s < ST − L_e. Since T ≠ N in the paper's own examples (T = 18.375 vs N = 16; T = 46 vs N = 32), SN and ST are different quantities and the interval in Section IV-A-1 is wrong.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section V-1, "we set T = 18.375" (and T used in Eqs. (3)-(7))
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: T is defined as a matrix dimension (F_b ∈ C^{T×T}, T_b is an N×T matrix, f_{b,n} ∈ C^{1×T}, oversampled f^{(S)}_{b,n} ∈ C^{1×ST}). A dimension/number of samples must be an integer, yet the paper sets T = 18.375. The stated model cannot be instantiated with a non-integer T; the relationship between T, the sampling grid and the matrix formulation is never reconciled.

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract ("MA-TISK does not require beam alignment") vs. Section IV-B
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The abstract claims the scheme "does not require beam alignment," contrasting it with proposals using analog beamforming at both transmitter and receiver. However, Section IV-B specifies "a receiver employing analog beamforming towards the transmitter," which necessarily requires receive beam alignment. The claim is only valid for the transmitter side and is overstated as written.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section V-1 ("Rectangular Pulse Shape"), description of RC-lowpass effect
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: "We take a rectangular pulse of duration 21.8 ns and a first order RC-lowpass filter with cut-off frequency 50 MHz ... The RC-lowpass filter distorts the rectangular pulses to an almost triangular shape and the transition period extends significantly beyond the duration of the pulse." A first-order RC filter with f_c = 50 MHz has time constant τ = 1/(2π f_c) ≈ 3.2 ns, i.e. about 1/7 of the 21.8 ns pulse. The filtered pulse would be essentially trapezoidal (nearly rectangular with rounded edges) with a tail of ~10 ns, not "almost triangular" with a transition extending significantly beyond the pulse.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section V-2 ("signal-to-interference-and-noise-ratio (SINR)") vs. Section V-1 ("No Gaussian noise was added")
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Section V-1 explicitly states "No Gaussian noise was added. Interference is solely due to crosstalk of subcarriers and intersymbol interference" and reports SIR. Section V-2 reports the same type of simulation result but labels it SINR (signal-to-interference-and-noise ratio). With no noise in the simulation, the quantity cannot be an SINR; the two sections report nominally different metrics for the same experiment.

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract ("MA-TISK does not suffer from spectral re-growth issues plaguing other constant envelope modulations like GMSK")
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The body shows that spectral regrowth is not eliminated but merely steered in-band, where it degrades the SIR to 18.3 dB (first example). Moreover, the paper itself reports that GMSK-type pulses were tried and "we were unable to identify any significant differences compared to squared sine-wave pulses," which undercuts the claimed advantage over GMSK.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section IV-B (receiver), "Even for three or more separable propagation paths, two receiver chains are sufficient to equalize the resulting intersymbol interference."
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: This assertion is made without derivation, simulation or citation supporting the specific claim that exactly two receive chains suffice for an arbitrary number (three or more) of separable paths. No results in Section V address multipath equalization, so the claim is unsupported by the reported evidence.
